title: Gradle
description: Build lifecycle, dependency configurations, caching, version catalogs and Android variants.

questions.question: Which are the three phases of a Gradle build?
questions.explanation: Initialization finds projects (settings file), configuration builds the task graph, execution runs tasks.

questions.question: In which phase is settings.gradle(.kts) evaluated?
questions.explanation: The settings file decides which projects take part in the build.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'api' and 'implementation' (java-library plugin)?

answers.text: 'api' dependencies leak to consumers' compile classpath; 'implementation' ones don't

questions.explanation: Prefer implementation: fewer recompilations and better encapsulation.

questions.question: What does the configuration cache do?

answers.text: Caches the result of the configuration phase and reuses it

questions.explanation: The build cache stores task outputs; the configuration cache stores the configured task graph.

questions.question: What does the build cache allow?

answers.text: Reusing task outputs from earlier builds, also from other machines (remote cache)

questions.explanation: Cacheable tasks with declared inputs/outputs can be loaded from cache instead of executed.

questions.question: Which files belong to the Gradle wrapper and should be committed?
questions.explanation: The wrapper pins the Gradle version (distributionUrl) so everybody builds with the same one.

questions.question: Which sections can gradle/libs.versions.toml contain?
questions.explanation: There is also [bundles] for groups of libraries.

questions.question: Why prefer tasks.register(...) over tasks.create(...)?

answers.text: register is lazy: the task is only configured if it's needed
create is deprecated in Kotlin only

questions.explanation: Task configuration avoidance reduces configuration time in large builds.

questions.question: How does Gradle resolve a version conflict between two transitive dependencies by default?

answers.text: It picks the nearest one in the graph, like Maven

questions.explanation: Use constraints, platforms or resolutionStrategy to influence it; dependencyInsight explains the choice.

questions.question: Which command shows why a specific dependency version was selected?
questions.explanation: Add --configuration (e.g. releaseRuntimeClasspath) to inspect a specific classpath.

questions.question: What is a common way to share build logic between modules today?

answers.text: Convention plugins in an included build (e.g. build-logic)
buildSrc also works, but invalidates more on change
Copying build scripts into every module

questions.explanation: Included builds via includeBuild() are preferred for large projects.

questions.question: What are the benefits of the Provider API (Property<T>, Provider<T>)?

answers.text: Values are computed lazily, when needed
Task dependencies can be inferred from wiring
It makes builds run without the daemon

questions.explanation: Wiring outputs of one task to inputs of another via providers adds the dependency automatically.

questions.question: Android: how are build variants formed?

answers.text: Build types × product flavors (per flavor dimension)

questions.explanation: Example: flavors 'free'/'paid' × build types 'debug'/'release' = 4 variants.

questions.question: What is the difference between testImplementation and androidTestImplementation?

answers.text: testImplementation: local JVM unit tests; androidTestImplementation: instrumented tests on a device
androidTestImplementation is only for release builds

questions.explanation: Local tests run in src/test; instrumented tests in src/androidTest.

questions.question: Why is KSP usually preferred over kapt?

answers.text: It processes Kotlin directly without generating Java stubs, which is faster

questions.explanation: kapt is in maintenance mode; Room, Moshi, Hilt and others support KSP.

questions.question: What is the difference between dependsOn, mustRunAfter and finalizedBy?

answers.text: dependsOn: the other task is required and runs first
mustRunAfter: only ordering if both are scheduled
finalizedBy: the other task runs afterwards, even if this one fails

questions.explanation: Only dependsOn adds a task to the graph; mustRunAfter only orders tasks that are already scheduled.

questions.question: Which gradle.properties settings commonly speed up builds?
questions.explanation: org.gradle.debug makes the build wait for a debugger instead.

questions.question: What decides if a task is UP-TO-DATE?

answers.text: Its declared inputs and outputs haven't changed since the last run
The task ran less than 24 hours ago
The Git commit is the same

questions.explanation: Tasks without declared outputs are never up to date.

questions.question: What does './gradlew build --scan' do?

answers.text: Publishes a Build Scan with timing, dependency and failure details
Scans the code for security issues

questions.explanation: Build Scans help find slow tasks, cache misses and configuration time.

questions.question: What is a composite build?

answers.text: A build that includes other complete builds via includeBuild()
A build with more than one subproject
A build that runs on several machines

questions.explanation: Included builds can substitute binary dependencies with project sources, e.g. for a library you're changing.
